verdict_reasoning: Level 1b fails on three fixable objections. The main argument is psql completion, but the proposal does not say why psql cannot use the text after the cursor (already-exists-1). The only outside demand is for the v1 order, which v2 rejects (demand-1). Message #4 says completion centers on a single relation (prior-attempts-1). The goal may be fine, and the thread has one supporter, so this is a discussion to finish before code review.

brief.title: Allow FROM before SELECT, with the select list last or omitted
brief.problem: Postgres requires a query to start with SELECT, so psql cannot complete column names in the select list: the completer sees only text left of the cursor, and the tables come later. The author frames this as help for interactive users, and admits the real motivation is partly "just for fun".
brief.proposed_design: v2 lets a query start with FROM, followed by WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and WINDOW in their usual order, then the select list, then ORDER BY, LIMIT and locking clauses. An omitted SELECT means SELECT *. The grammar builds the same SelectStmt as the standard form, so nothing below the parser changes; v1 instead put the select list right after FROM.
user_visible_surface: New query syntax: FROM from_item [other clauses] SELECT select_list, accepted wherever a SELECT is, including sub-selects, CTEs, set operations and INSERT ... SELECT.
Bare FROM with SELECT omitted means SELECT *, for example FROM films WHERE ...
PL/pgSQL recognizes FROM as the start of a SQL statement.
psql tab completion offers FROM as a command start and completes columns in the select list and in GROUP BY.
New sections in the SELECT reference page, including a Compatibility note calling the form a PostgreSQL extension.
author_claims: The new productions add no grammar conflicts and change nothing below the parser.
Stored queries and pg_get_viewdef output show the standard form.
FROM-first order lets psql complete select-list columns, which is impossible when SELECT comes first.
Select-list-last is easier to teach than allowing the select list in several positions.
The standard will never move SELECT, so Postgres is free to define this extension.
brief.thread_state: Vik Fearing supports the idea and prefers SELECT after HAVING, which v2 adopts. Denis Smirnov prefers v1 for DuckDB and ClickHouse compatibility and output-alias completion in GROUP BY, and asks for JOIN completion tests; Peter Eisentraut is the listed committer but has not posted.
unclear: v2 matches no other system, so queries written for DuckDB or ClickHouse in v1 order fail; the thread has not chosen between v1 and v2.
The material does not say whether 0002 psql completion was updated for v2 placement or what it tests.
The proposal does not say how FROM-first queries complete columns with joins, aliases or qualified names.
The proposal does not say how a bare FROM interacts with set operations, parenthesized queries or ambiguity with existing statements starting with FROM.
The proposal does not show whether the new grammar affects parser size or speed.
No user demand beyond the author's teaching sessions and the completion argument is shown.

prior_attempts.title: Tab completion for SELECT in psql
prior_attempts.quote: I think the completion needs to be smarter to be acceptable.
prior_attempts.reason: Heikki Linnakangas found the completions both too broad and too narrow: system catalog columns flood short prefixes, the FROM clause is ignored, and system columns appear inconsistently. He held that the completion must be smarter to be acceptable. He also reported that the query on pg_attribute took about 1 second on a database with a 1000-partition table. An earlier review by Peter Eisentraut found broken older-version queries and an unsettled function filter. The rebased patch of 2018-09-22 got no visible reply before the entry was returned.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P3 completed select-list columns without knowing the tables. This proposal changes the grammar so the tables are named first and completion can use them.

objections.title: A psql completion gap is being fixed with server grammar
objections.failure_scenario: An application developer pastes a FROM-first query from a psql session into application code. A SQL linter or proxy that embeds a Postgres-compatible parser rejects it, and the developer learns this only at deploy time. The only stated gain was select-list completion inside psql.
objections.argument: Message #1 and the 0002 commit message present completion as the practical argument. They say the completer sees only text left of the cursor. That is a design choice in psql's tab-complete code: readline also exposes the rest of the line, and a client such as pgcli reads the whole buffer and offers select-list columns for SELECT ... FROM t. A committer would likely ask why a client-side limit justifies a permanent server grammar extension.
objections.author_must_show: Why can psql not read the text after the cursor, for example a typed "SELECT  FROM t", to complete select-list columns without any grammar change?

critic.reasoning: Readline gives psql the whole line buffer, so the claim that a client "has no way" to complete the select list is too strong. The proposal does not say why a client-side change would not do.

objections.title: Demand shown is for v1 order, but v2 ships an order nobody uses
objections.failure_scenario: A DuckDB or ClickHouse user pastes `FROM films SELECT title WHERE len > '02:00'` into psql and gets a syntax error. The only outside users who already write FROM-first queries cannot reuse them. The v2 form is then used only by people who learn it fresh from the Postgres docs.
objections.argument: The only demand outside the thread is that two other systems ship the v1 placement (messages #1 and #3). Message #3 admits that "nobody ... ships the placement in v2-patch grammar", and message #4 asks for v1 for that reason. The rest of the demand is the author's teaching sessions and the stated motivation "just for fun" (message #1). No -general or -bugs reports and no user requests appear in the material.
objections.author_must_show: Which users outside this thread have asked for FROM-first queries in Postgres, and which placement do they actually write today?

critic.reasoning: Two other systems shipping FROM-first counts as demand evidence, but only for the v1 order. For v2 the material shows the author's teaching sessions and one supportive reply, with no user requests.

objections.title: Completion argument may repeat the quality gap that stalled earlier select-list completion
objections.failure_scenario: A user writes `from orders o join customers c using (id) select ` and presses tab. psql offers columns of one table only, or bare names that are ambiguous across both. The permanent grammar extension is then in the release, but the completion that justified it falls short in the common multi-table case.
objections.argument: Message #1 presents 0002 as "the actual pro-argument", and the commit message calls it "the practical argument". [P3] stalled because reviewers found select-list completion too broad and too narrow, and its key sentence asked for smarter completion. Message #4 reports that the current rules are "mostly centered on a single relation" and asks for tests with joins, aliases and qualified names. The material does not show that 0002 was updated for v2 placement, so the main benefit is not yet shown for the queries users write.
objections.author_must_show: How does the v2 completion behave for joins, table aliases and qualified columns, and do the tests cover those cases?

precedents.title: Tab completion for SELECT in psql

critic.reasoning: Message #4 says the rules center on a single relation, and nothing in the thread answers it. Two supports are weak: [P3] ignored FROM, which this patch knows, and v2-0001 does touch tab-complete.in.c and its test.

other_surviving.title: v2 clause order matches no other system and fixes a third dialect
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user copies `FROM films SELECT title WHERE len > '02:00'` from DuckDB or ClickHouse into psql and gets a syntax error, because v2 only accepts the select list last. Once v2 ships, adding v1 placement later means mixed rules in the grammar, and taking v2 back would break the queries users already wrote.
other_surviving.argument: Message #3 says DuckDB and ClickHouse both use v1 placement and that no system uses v2. The CommitFest entry for this feature is titled 'FROM clause before SELECT', yet v2 is a spelling no other system has. Message #4 prefers v1 for compatibility, and the thread has not decided. The 'easier to teach' reason in message #3 concerns one design choice, but the project would have to defend the resulting spelling for as long as it exists.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why should Postgres define a select-list-last order that no other system accepts, instead of the v1 order that existing FROM-first users already write?

critic.reasoning: Message #3 itself says DuckDB and ClickHouse queries fail under v2 and that no system ships the v2 order. Message #4 prefers v1, and the thread has not chosen.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Bare FROM adds a second SELECT * shorthand next to TABLE
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A reader sees `FROM films`, `TABLE films` and `SELECT * FROM films` in one codebase and has to learn three spellings of the same query. A mistyped or truncated statement that ends after its FROM clause runs as SELECT * and returns every row instead of raising a syntax error.
other_surviving.argument: The doc hunk itself calls `FROM films` 'much like TABLE films', so Postgres already has a shorthand for this. The completion argument in message #1 does not need an omitted SELECT, because completion happens while SELECT is still being typed. The proposal gives no reason for the bare form beyond the DuckDB example in message #1, and v2 already departs from DuckDB.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What does the bare FROM form give users that TABLE and the FROM ... SELECT form do not, and is it worth the risk of truncated statements silently running?

critic.reasoning: The doc hunk says bare FROM, unlike TABLE, takes WHERE, so it is more than a duplicate. But the completion argument does not need an omitted SELECT, and the proposal gives no other reason for it.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: A second query grammar that every future SELECT clause must track
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later patch adds a clause to SELECT, such as a new standard grouping or row-pattern clause, and edits only the standard production in gram.y. The clause works in SELECT-first queries and gives a syntax error in FROM-first ones. Nobody notices until a user reports it, because no test compares the two spellings.
other_surviving.argument: v2 adds parallel productions in gram.y and pl_gram.y that must reproduce the clause order of simple_select. The commit message says the productions build the same SelectStmt, which protects the code below the parser but does nothing for future grammar edits. The proposal names no check that fails when the two spellings drift apart. Every later SELECT feature carries this cost, whether or not its author uses FROM-first.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What mechanism or test makes a future SELECT clause fail loudly if it is added to the standard spelling but not to the FROM-first spelling?

critic.reasoning: The proposal names no check that catches drift between the two spellings. Two points soften it: simple_select already has parallel productions, and the material only says pl_gram.y recognizes FROM as a statement start.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Permanent SQL syntax added to work around a psql completer limit
refuted.failure_scenario: The project commits to a non-standard query form in every grammar, in PL/pgSQL, and in the docs. The main stated gain is that psql, which reads only the text left of the cursor, can complete one clause. Users of editors and IDEs that see the whole buffer gain nothing, and psql completion with joins and aliases is not yet shown.
refuted.argument: Messages #1 and #3 rest the case on psql completion, and message #1 says the real motivation is 'just for fun'. Message #4 notes that the completion rules center on a single relation and asks for join, alias and qualified-name tests. [P3] stalled because column completion was not smart enough to be useful. Here FROM is known, which removes part of that problem but not the multi-relation case.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users, beyond psql users typing single-table queries, have asked for this, and does psql complete correctly with joins, aliases and qualified columns?

precedents.title: Tab completion for SELECT in psql

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which makes the same point about a client-side limit with a more concrete question. Its completion part repeats prior-attempts-1.

refuted.title: v2 placement matches no other system and cannot change once shipped
refuted.failure_scenario: Postgres ships v2. Users store FROM-first queries in PL/pgSQL function bodies and in application code. Later the project wants DuckDB and ClickHouse compatibility, or the standard defines a FROM-first form, and finds that v1 placement or the standard form conflicts with v2 queries already in the field.
refuted.argument: Message #3 says DuckDB and ClickHouse use v1 placement and nobody ships v2. Message #4 prefers v1, and the thread has not settled the choice. PL/pgSQL stores function bodies as source text, so once the spelling ships it is frozen. Message #2 says the standard will not move SELECT, but [P8] was rejected partly for its risk of future conflicts with the standard.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is a placement that no other system uses the one Postgres should commit to permanently, given that the thread has not settled v1 against v2?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. Its added scenario does not hold, because adding v1 placement later would not break stored v2 queries, and [P8] concerned a keyword the standard already listed.

refuted.title: Small completion gain weighed against a permanent syntax extension
refuted.failure_scenario: The same reasoning admits ORDER BY ALL, SELECT * EXCLUDE and trailing commas, which message #1 lists as next candidates. Each adds productions and a documentation section, so the SELECT grammar grows a dialect layer. The psql benefit stays limited, because completion handles mostly a single relation.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says the gain is "one clause wide" and that the motivation is partly "just for fun". The only demand shown comes from the author's teaching sessions. Message #4 says the completion rules center on a single relation and asks for JOIN and alias cases. [P3] was returned because completion needed to be smarter to be acceptable, and that is the main argument here too.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users outside teaching sessions have asked for this, and does completion work for multi-table joins with aliases and qualified columns?

precedents.title: Tab completion for SELECT in psql

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1 for the missing demand and of prior-attempts-1 for join completion. Its accumulation part repeats demand-3.

refuted.title: Bare FROM duplicates TABLE and SELECT * with little saved
refuted.failure_scenario: A reader of an SQL file finds "FROM films", "TABLE films" and "SELECT * FROM films" used side by side. All three mean the same query. Tools, books and reviewers then have to know and accept a third spelling that only Postgres and a few other systems use, and each in a different clause order.
refuted.argument: The SELECT reference page already has TABLE films for the bare case. SELECT * FROM covers the case with WHERE at the cost of nine characters. The documentation hunk calls bare FROM "much like TABLE films", so it adds a second way to do an existing job. As in [P8], the new syntax is handy but not much better than what exists.
refuted.author_must_show: What does omitting SELECT give users beyond TABLE and SELECT *, apart from saving a few keystrokes?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-3, which adds a concrete scenario. [P8] must not be used as support, since its recorded reason was a keyword conflict with the standard.

refuted.title: Gain is one psql clause, cost falls on every SQL parser
refuted.failure_scenario: An application stores `FROM orders WHERE ...` in a function body. External tools that parse Postgres SQL, such as linters, syntax highlighters, query rewriters and migration diff tools, reject it or misread it. Their maintainers find out from bug reports after the release.
refuted.argument: Message #1 limits the payoff to psql completion in the select list ("the gain is one clause wide"). Message #4 reports that join cases, aliases and qualified columns are not yet covered, so even that gain is narrow. The new grammar is accepted everywhere a SELECT is, including PL/pgSQL, so every tool that parses Postgres SQL must learn it. The material does not weigh that cost against the completion gain.
refuted.author_must_show: How many users would use FROM-first queries for completion, measured against the number of tools that must learn the new syntax?

critic.reasoning: Every grammar addition, including standard ones such as MERGE, requires external parsers to catch up. Nothing ties this cost to this proposal, and the project does not carry it.

refuted.title: The case for this applies equally to the friendly-SQL list
refuted.failure_scenario: After this commit, proposals for ORDER BY ALL, SELECT * EXCLUDE and trailing commas each cite "the standard will never do this, other systems have it". Each one adds permanent non-standard grammar. Reviewers then have no rule left for rejecting any of them.
refuted.argument: Message #1 names that list and defers it as "separate discussions". The case made here (convenience, the standard leaves the spelling free, as Vik says in message #2, plus another system has it) fits each item on that list just as well. A committer would likely ask what makes this extension different from the next ten.
refuted.author_must_show: What criterion separates FROM-first from ORDER BY ALL, EXCLUDE and trailing commas, so that accepting this one does not commit Postgres to the rest?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 gives the criterion: the surface is "tied to the completion argument", which ORDER BY ALL, EXCLUDE and trailing commas lack. The message leaves those out as separate discussions.

committability.liability: A non-standard query spelling that cannot be removed once users write it, plus parallel grammar productions and psql completion rules to keep in step with every later SELECT change.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 one day after the first review and moved the entry to the next CommitFest. Message #1 also says he will drop the patch if consensus is against non-standard grammar.

SELECT ...".; Fix use of relcache TriggerDesc field introduced by commit 05c8482f7f.

To allow inserts in parallel-mode this feature has to ensure that all the
constraints, triggers, etc. are parallel-safe for the partition hierarchy
which is costly and we need to find a better way to do that. Additionally,
we could have used existing cached information in some cases like indexes,

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallel INSERT (INTO ... SELECT ...)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set allows parallel execution of both the INSERT and the SELECT parts of "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ...", with workers inserting tuples themselves; where parallel insert is unsafe (for example foreign keys or ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE), only the SELECT part is parallelised. It changes the planner, executor and parallel-worker code, adds parallel-safety checks on the target table (including partitions, triggers and domains), and adds a GUC and a reloption to control the feature.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Parts of the work, "Parallel SELECT for INSERT" and the related GUC/reloption, were committed during the thread. The remaining patches, which add the parallel INSERT functionality itself, were marked Returned with Feedback because of feedback given on pgsql-committers, which said a lot of work remained. The visible messages do not show the content of that feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There is a lot of work
to do for this patch as per the feedback given on pgsql-committers
[1].

precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds psql tab completion after SELECT, suggesting column names from all visible tables and function names. Functions that are unlikely to be called directly are filtered out, and later versions use per-server-version queries and add completion after commas.

He held that the completion must be smarter to be acceptable. He also reported that the query on pg_attribute took about 1 second on a database with a 1000-partition table. An earlier review by Peter Eisentraut found broken older-version queries and an unsettled function filter. The rebased patch of 2018-09-22 got no visible reply before the entry was returned.

precedents_retrieved.title: INSERT .. ON CONFLICT DO SELECT
precedents_retrieved.summary: INSERT .. ON CONFLICT DO SELECT

precedents_retrieved.title: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT [FOR ...]
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds ON CONFLICT DO SELECT to INSERT, which returns the conflicting row through RETURNING instead of updating it, with an optional row lock (DO SELECT FOR UPDATE and similar). It revives a 2017 patch by Marko and rebases it for table AMs, EXPLAIN, RLS and OLD/NEW in RETURNING.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed found the patch not yet committable. Partitioned tables crashed with DO SELECT FOR UPDATE, the docs did not cover DO SELECT, and regression and isolation tests were missing. The author agreed and said a new version would follow, but none was posted before the entry was closed in August 2025.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think there is still a fair bit more to do to get this into a
committable state. The docs in particular need work.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove redundant NULL check in clause_selectivity_ext()
precedents_retrieved.summary: Remove the NULL clause check in clause_selectivity_ext(), which carries a "can this still happen?" comment, because no core caller seems to pass a NULL clause. The author listed each core call site to support this.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane wanted the check kept because it is cheap and extensions call clauselist_selectivity and related functions and may rely on it not crashing on a NULL. He also said the list_length check proves nothing about NULL list elements, and that removing such checks one at a time without agreed invariants is not wise. David Rowley agreed, saying no speedup could be measured and no benchmark was given, and suggested marking the entry rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Certainly, such an assumption could be argued to be a bug they
should fix; but I'm disinclined to make them jump through that
hoop for a vanishingly small performance improvement.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add SQL syntax check
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a --syntax option to the postgres server binary that reads SQL from standard input, runs it through the raw parser only (no catalog access or parse analysis), and reports whether it is valid SQL via a message and exit code. The intent was to support manual and automated script checks and editor integrations.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Several reviewers held that the feature did not belong in the postgres binary, and Robert Haas marked the entry Rejected on that basis. The main objection, attributed to Tom Lane and endorsed by Robert Haas, was that the check exposes an implementation detail, the division of work between gram.y (raw_parser) and parse analysis, so it would miss things users consider syntax errors and flag things that seem semantic. Making that work would need a much larger effort and a different design. Robert Haas also noted that the 45-line patch had no comments, tests or documentation, and the author agreed to the rejection.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I strongly suspect that doing something useful in this area requires
about two orders of magnitude more code than are included in this
patch, and a completely different design.

precedents_retrieved.title: MAP syntax for arrays
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Andreas Karlsson, Ashutosh Bapat
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a new expression type and syntax MAP(<func_name> OVER <array_expression>) that applies a function to each element of an array and returns the resulting array, reusing the existing array-coercion infrastructure. The author also considered a more general form mapping an arbitrary expression over an array, and reported better performance than the unnest/array_agg subquery approach for small arrays.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to adding proprietary syntax that could conflict with future SQL standard use of the MAP keyword, which is already a non-reserved keyword in SQL:2016. They also judged the syntax not much better than the existing sub-select with unnest and array_agg, which is more flexible (for example, it allows a WHERE filter), and suggested optimizing the unnest/array_agg combination in the planner instead of adding new syntax. Heikki Linnakangas summarized the consensus as not wanting the feature and marked the entry Rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Yeah, it's a
handy syntax, but it's not that much better than using a subselect or a
writing a user-defined function. And there's risk of future conflicts
with the SQL standard.

precedents_retrieved.title: Boolean partition syntax
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the grammar of the partition FOR VALUES clause so that the Boolean literals true and false are accepted as partition bound values, which previously produced a syntax error. Later in the thread a broader alternative was posted that restricts partition bounds to the AexprConst grammar and coerces them during parse analysis.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The discussion moved from the narrow Boolean-literal fix to whether partition bounds should be parsed more generally, for example as expressions evaluated and checked for constancy, and senior developers disagreed with the patch's design. The alternative AexprConst-based patch was not reviewed and was found to reject negative numbers. With the final commitfest in progress and no updated patch, the entry was marked Returned with Feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Given the current state of this patch, with a number of senior
developers disagreeing with the design, and the last CF being in
progress, I think we should mark this as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Ltree syntax improvement
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch extends the set of characters allowed in ltree labels by adding two escaping mechanisms, backslash-escaping of individual characters and double-quoting of whole labels, for the ltree, lquery and ltxtquery datatypes. Later versions refactored the label parsing into common code shared by the three types.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to the design of having both quoting and backslash-escaping and proposed SQL-identifier-style quoting instead. He also questioned the stripping of leading and trailing whitespace, the structure of ltree_io.c (several routines that depend on the quoting rules and must stay in sync, plus multiple passes over the input), and changes to error reporting. After a later request to rebase, no new version was submitted for two months, and Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As I mentioned upthread, I'm not convinced that we ought to have
*both* quoting and backslash-escaping in these datatypes.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert support for improved tracking of nested queries
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert support for improved tracking of nested queries
Reverted commit(s): Track more precisely query locations for nested statements; Fix regression with location calculation of nested statements; pg_stat_statements: Add tests for nested queries with level tracking
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts the two following commits:
- 499edb09741b, track more precisely query locations for nested
statements.
- 06450c7b8c70, a follow-up fix of 499edb09741b with query locations.
The test introduced in this commit is not reverted.  This is proving
useful to track a problem that only pgaudit was able to detect.

These prove to have issues with the tracking of SELECT statements, when
these use multiple parenthesis which is something supported by the
grammar.  Incorrect location and lengths are causing pg_stat_statements
to become confused, failing its job in query normalization with
potential out-of-bound writes because the location and the length may
not match with what can be handled.  A lot of the query patterns
discussed when this issue was reported have no test coverage in the main
regression test suite, or the recovery test 027_stream_regress.pl would
have caught the problems as pg_stat_statements is loaded by the node
running the regression tests.  A first step would be to improve the test
coverage to stress more the query normalization logic.

A different portion of this work was done in 45e0ba30fc40, with the
addition of tests for nested queries.  These can be left in the tree.
They are useful to track the way inner queries are currently tracked by
PGSS with non-top-level entries, and will be useful when reconsidering
in the future the work reverted here.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent proposes FROM-first or select-list-last syntax. [P8]'s standard-conflict reason is weak here because FROM is already reserved, so I raise no objection on it.
Not applicable. pg_dump and pg_get_viewdef output stays in the standard form, so this review raises no round-trip objection.

The proposal adds no persistent or cross-node state. The grammar builds the same SelectStmt, so catalogs, WAL, on-disk format, the wire protocol and replication are untouched, and stored views and BEGIN ATOMIC bodies deparse to the standard form. Text-stored function bodies keep the new spelling and will not load on older servers, but the same holds for any new syntax.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. The new spelling builds the same SelectStmt as the standard form, so permission checks, RLS, column privileges and security barrier views apply unchanged. psql completion reads column names from catalogs that are already readable by every user.
Objections are listed above. There is no hot-path cost: the change is limited to the parser. The listed committer has not posted yet.
Two objections raised from the already-exists angle.
Demand is thin but not shown to be absent, so all objections are "not now, show demand" and fixable.
